purpose: Authored three-line in-game summaries. Full lessons and source attribution remain in the history audit, gallery, and generated source tooltip.

lines: Oakley joined Buffalo Bill's Wild West in 1885.
Her marksmanship was a professional exhibition.
Stage dress was not everyday frontier clothing.
Assayers measured precious metals in mine samples.
Denver had a U.S. assay office by 1870.
This linked mining with bullion valuation.
Alfred Nobel patented dynamite in 1867.
Its manufacture expanded in the following years.
Powder Pike is a fictional blasting worker.
In 1878, a Lincoln County War faction burned
Alexander McSween's house in New Mexico.
This fictional arsonist is not a documented person.
Bartenders learned a wide range of mixed drinks.
Jerry Thomas's guide records period recipes
and skilled professional drink preparation.
Born enslaved, Reeves became a deputy in 1875.
He served in Indian Territory and Arkansas.
Popular arrest and killing totals are disputed.
Billy the Kid died in New Mexico in 1881.
Court, government and newspaper records survive.
These outweigh later screen portrayals and myths.
Louis Southworth worked as a blacksmith in
Buena Vista, Oregon, in 1870. He documents Black
skilled work; this composite is not his portrait.
Express companies offered rewards for criminals.
Wells Fargo agents worked with sheriffs.
Their role differed from statutory arrest powers.
Black Army regiments were established in 1866.
They guarded travel routes at Western posts
and enforced U.S. expansion against Native peoples.
An 1874 print shows builders using hand tools.
Folding measuring rules also predate this era.
Carpentry required measurement and joinery.
Goodnight and Loving drove cattle from Texas
toward Fort Sumner in 1866. Goodnight later
established ranches in the Texas Panhandle.
Union veterans founded the Grand Army of the
Republic in 1866 to support fellow veterans.
A blue coat alone cannot prove wartime service.
The Mining Law of 1872 formalized mineral claims.
Discovery, location and surveys mattered legally.
A paper or pistol does not prove claim jumping.
Express messengers guarded stagecoach valuables.
They commonly rode beside the driver.
Guarding cargo distinguished their work.
Soapy Smith's gang operated in Skagway during
the Klondike rush. In 1898 he used the building
now preserved as Jeff. Smiths Parlor.
Ashby is fictional. Executives such as Stanford
directed rail expansion. Southern Pacific's
southern transcontinental line was complete in 1883.
Doc Holliday trained as a dentist and moved west
with tuberculosis. He became a gambler and
joined the Earps in the 1881 Tombstone gunfight.
Black cowboys worked cattle after emancipation.
Nat Love and Bose Ikard rode Western trails.
This drover is a fictional composite.
Hickok fought Davis Tutt in Springfield in 1865.
Formal quick-draw showdowns were rare.
Later fiction made them seem more typical.
This fictional gunner depicts a frontier crewman.
Period Gatling guns used wheeled field carriages.
Hand cranking drove their rotating barrel cluster.
Mounted contract carriers served postal routes.
Horseback mail outlasted the Pony Express.
This courier and the rescue ability are fictional.
Protestant ministers founded Western churches.
Sheldon Jackson's papers document mission work.
This preacher's violent card ability is fiction.
Hispano families settled Colorado's San Luis Valley.
The Trujillo homesteads preserve their ranching
history and adobe and log-building traditions.
James was a former Confederate guerrilla who
robbed banks, trains and stagecoaches.
His crimes harmed civilians despite heroic myths.
Physicians used opium preparations for pain.
In the 1876 Little Bighorn campaign, Henry Porter
treated wounded men with laudanum and morphine.
Lozen, a Chiricahua Apache warrior, was
Victorio's sister. After his death she resisted,
then surrendered with Geronimo's band in 1886.
Blind Boone played with Black saloon musicians
in 1870s Missouri. Around 1880 he began touring
with John Lange Jr. This pianist is fictional.
Pinkerton agents investigated robberies and
worked for railroads and other private clients.
Some work involved labor disputes and spying.
Alice Ivers Tubbs made her living by gambling
in Western towns. Her career led from Colorado
mining communities to Deadwood by 1892.
Placer miners panned stream deposits for gold.
An 1889 photograph records this work at
Rockerville, Dakota Territory.
Quanah brought his Comanche followers to Fort Sill
in 1875. He later negotiated reservation life
and developed cattle-ranching interests.
At Wilcox, Wyoming, in June 1899, robbers used
explosives on a train's express car.
A major pursuit followed. This outlaw is fictional.
After Tunstall's murder in 1878, his followers
and McSween's became the Regulators.
Rival factions escalated the Lincoln County War.
Seven women joined the Salvation Army's official
U.S. mission in 1880; it reached California in 1883.
This organizer reflects women's religious work.
Managing cattle crews required practical work.
Thomas Hooban's 1880-81 ranch ledger records
workers' wages, cattle and supplies.
Disputes over unbranded cattle fueled conflict
in 1880s-1890s Wyoming. An accusation of rustling
did not prove theft. This cattle thief is fictional.
Winnemucca interpreted and advocated for Paiutes.
After forced removal from Malheur to Yakama,
she campaigned for their return and rights.
Sharps rifles served hunters and target shooters.
The 1879 catalog offered open, globe and vernier
iron sights. This marksman is fictional.
Horn was a freighter, cowboy and army scout.
He joined Pinkerton around 1890, then worked
for Wyoming cattle interests in the 1890s.
This avenger is fictional, not a documented hero.
Vigilantes punished people outside courts.
Their acts could include coercion and murder.
Jenny Fletcher helped build Nicodemus, Kansas.
She taught its first school and joined its AME
congregation from 1879. This organizer is fictional.
Montana vigilantes acted outside ordinary courts.
Punishments included banishment and killing.
Their claimed motives remain debated.
The Homestead Act of 1862 let eligible women
claim land and protected a claimant's widow.
Frontier landholding was not exclusively male.
Hickok served as a Kansas lawman and died in
Deadwood in 1876. Performance and storytelling
grew his legend beyond eyewitness history.
Wyatt joined Virgil, Morgan and Doc Holliday in
Tombstone's October 26, 1881 gunfight.
Virgil was marshal; Wyatt was not sole leader.
